In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the effect of afforestation has been to increase the acidity of the stream water in the two catchments studied.
the impact of afforestation is not a simple function of age but is dependent on site preparation, deposition changes, forest type, soil type and the interaction of these factors.
afforestation has a small effect on surface water acidification in the long term and this is only evident at a site that has been affected by past acidification.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
forest age and forest species have an impact on water quality, but the effect of the forest is less than anticipated and the impact is less severe than in other regions in Britain.

afforestation can have a marked impact on stream-water chemistry, which may be ameliorated by the natural acid buffering capacity of the soil, the extent of site preparation and the amount of deposition change during the forest development.
forest growth has had a significant effect on stream-water quality, and that the impact of afforestation has been exacerbated by deposition changes during forest growth.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the impact of afforestation is dependent on forest age and that the impact is likely to be less than that of other land use changes such as the conversion of moorland to agriculture.
the effects of afforestation on catchment water quality are complex, and are not solely driven by the age of the forest.

afforestation has the potential to increase the pH of streams and rivers in areas where the natural pH is below neutral, but this effect is likely to be small in comparison to the impact of deposition and land-use change.
